decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files do not yet exist for d5c3b5a4bfad618a. Segal (1970) re-tests Lenski (1967, Status Inconsistency and the Vote) using six combined Canadian surveys (1965-1967) and Multiple Classification Analysis. All four tested status inconsistency interaction terms (religion-education, religion-occupation, ethnicity-education, ethnicity-occupation) are statistically significant at the 0.01 level net of main status effects (Table I, p. 473). In the Conclusion, the author explicitly states the overall replication verdict that Lenski's findings were replicated to the extent of demonstrating statistically significant status inconsistency effects net of main status variables. The subsequent observation that main status effects (especially religion) are more powerfully related to party choice than inconsistency effects compares relative explanatory magnitudes (which Lenski's 2x2 tables did not separate) and does not report a failed replication of any tested original finding; per the codebook, a smaller or weaker effect size does not make a confirmed finding mixed.
